## Welcome {#home}

### Essential Medicines and Counterfeit Medicines

**Learning Objectives:**

- Define essential medicines and state WHO's selection criteria
- Describe India's National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM)
- State WHO's definition of rational use of medicines and list forms of irrational use
- Distinguish substandard, falsified, and generic medicines
- Explain why WHO retired the term "counterfeit medicines"

🟢 **MUST KNOW** · 🟡 **SHOULD KNOW** · 🟣 **MAY KNOW** · 🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.notes}
This chapter shifts focus from disease epidemiology to the medicines
supply chain — access, rational prescribing, and quality — as a
determinant of health-system performance.
:::

---

## What Are Essential Medicines? {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

**WHO definition:** essential medicines are those that satisfy the
**priority health care needs** of a population.

**Selection criteria:**

- Disease prevalence and public health relevance
- Evidence of clinical **efficacy and safety**
- Comparative **cost and cost-effectiveness**

The first WHO Model List of Essential Drugs was published in **1977**,
with 186 medicines, to help countries prioritize which medicines to
stock, procure, and make affordable at every level of care.

---

## India's National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM) {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

India adapts the WHO model into its own **National List of Essential
Medicines (NLEM)**, maintained under the **Central Drugs Standard Control
Organisation (CDSCO)** — India's National Regulatory Authority.

- First published 2011; most recently revised as **NLEM 2022**
  (384 medicines across 27 therapeutic categories)
- **Inclusion criteria:** approved/licensed in India, cost-effective, and
  stable under Indian storage conditions
- Purpose: ensure **accessibility of affordable, quality medicines** at
  every level of healthcare, and to guide public procurement and price
  control

---

## Rational Use of Medicines {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

**WHO definition (1985):** rational use means patients receive
medications appropriate to their clinical needs, in doses that meet
their individual requirements, for an adequate period of time, and at
the **lowest cost** to them and their community.

**The core criteria:**

- Appropriate **indication**
- Appropriate **medicine** choice
- Appropriate **dosage**
- Correctly **dispensed**
- Patient appropriately **informed**
- Patient **adherence**

---

## Forms of Irrational Use {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

Common patterns of irrational medicine use:

- **Polypharmacy** — using too many medicines per patient
- Inappropriate use of **antimicrobials** (wrong dose, for non-bacterial
  infections) — a major driver of antimicrobial resistance
- **Over-use of injections** where oral formulations would work
- Prescribing that doesn't follow **clinical guidelines**
- Inappropriate **self-medication**, often with prescription-only drugs
- **Non-adherence** to prescribed dosing regimens

**Scale of the problem:** WHO estimates more than half of all medicines
worldwide are prescribed, dispensed, or sold inappropriately, and half of
all patients fail to take them correctly.

---

## Substandard and Falsified Medical Products {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

In 2017, the World Health Assembly retired the term **"counterfeit
medicines"** in favour of **Substandard and Falsified (SF) medical
products**:

- **Substandard** — authorized medical products that fail to meet
  quality standards or specifications
- **Falsified** — products that deliberately and fraudulently
  misrepresent their identity, composition, or source

**Why the term changed:** "counterfeit" is a legal/intellectual-property
concept (trademark infringement) and doesn't necessarily indicate a
health risk. The new terms reframe the issue as a **public health
problem**, separate from patent and trademark disputes.

---

## Generic vs. Branded Medicines {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

- **Branded/innovator medicine** — sold under a manufacturer's trademark,
  often while under patent protection
- **Generic medicine** — a bioequivalent copy of an approved medicine,
  sold under its chemical/generic name (or a different brand) once patent
  protection expires, typically at much lower cost

Generic substitution is one of the most effective, low-cost levers for
improving access to essential medicines — most NLEM medicines are
available generically.

---

## Access to Medicines: Broader Determinants {background-color="#E8E4F3"}

🟣 **MAY KNOW**

Beyond the essential-medicines list itself, actual access depends on:

- **Rational selection and use** (covered above)
- **Sustainable financing** and affordable pricing
- **Reliable health and supply systems** (procurement, storage,
  distribution — including cold-chain where needed)
- Sound **regulatory systems** to keep substandard/falsified products out
  of the supply chain

These four pillars are the standard WHO framework for describing access
to essential medicines as a health-system, not just a pharmacological,
issue.

---

## The 2017 SSFFC-to-SF Terminology Shift {background-color="#E8E4F3"}

🟣 **MAY KNOW**

Before 2017, WHO used the unwieldy acronym **SSFFC**
(Substandard/Spurious/Falsely-labelled/Falsified/Counterfeit) medical
products. This was simplified to **SF (Substandard and Falsified)** at
the Seventieth World Health Assembly specifically to separate the public
health question (is this medicine safe and effective?) from
intellectual-property law (is this a trademark violation?) — two
questions that had previously been conflated under one confusing label.

This is an example of:

- Rational use of medicines
- [Irrational use of medicines]{.correct data-explanation="Inappropriate antimicrobial use for a non-bacterial (viral) infection, along with unnecessary polypharmacy, is a classic example of irrational medicine use."}
- Generic substitution
- A falsified medical product
:::

## Self-Check: Question 4 {background-color="#FDE8E8"}

🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.quiz-question}
### Question 4

WHO replaced the term "counterfeit medicines" with "Substandard and
Falsified (SF) medical products" in 2017 primarily because:

- Counterfeit medicines no longer exist
- ["Counterfeit" is a trademark/IP concept and doesn't necessarily indicate a health risk]{.correct data-explanation="The 2017 World Health Assembly decision reframed the issue as a public health concern, separate from intellectual-property/trademark law, which is what 'counterfeit' legally refers to."}
- SF is a shorter acronym
- Falsified medicines are always more dangerous than substandard ones
:::

🧡 **QUESTION**

specifications due to a manufacturing defect, without any intent to

- Falsified
- [Substandard]{.correct data-explanation="Substandard medical products are authorized products that fail to meet quality standards or specifications — distinct from falsified products, which involve deliberate misrepresentation."}

:::
